overview: Do not read this as a country founded in 1650 and ended in 1938. The atlas backfills one modern Hong Kong-shaped polygon across twelve snapshots from 1650, although the area then lay within Qing Xin'an County; its 1938 cutoff is a data handoff to a United Kingdom record, not the end of the colony. This card follows the communities around Victoria Harbour and today's New Territories through Qing coastal evacuation and resettlement, British seizure after the Opium Wars, a migrant port shaped by unequal colonial law and organized resistance, Japanese occupation, postwar industry and public housing, and the 1997 transfer to the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China. “Hong Kong” here means a changing place and population, not one unbroken sovereign state or one culture.

periods.title: Qing coast, villages and boats
periods.summary: The 1650 start is the atlas's first chosen snapshot, not Hong Kong's founding. Qing authorities emptied much of the coast in 1661 and reopened it in 1669; returning and new settlers rebuilt farming, fishing, lineage and boat communities in Xin'an County.

periods.title: War, cession and a new port
periods.summary: British forces occupied Hong Kong Island in 1841, and the 1842 Treaty of Nanking ceded it after Britain's victory in the First Opium War. The harbour became a colonial entrepot while Chinese migrants, merchants, labourers and families rapidly outnumbered the small European ruling population.

periods.title: Kowloon, urban growth and institutions
periods.summary: After the Second Opium War, the 1860 Convention of Peking ceded Kowloon south of Boundary Street. Reservoirs, schools, hospitals, roads, reclamation and shipping expanded, yet crowded tenements, scarce water and an appointed colonial government made improvement sharply unequal.

periods.title: New Territories lease, resistance and plague reform
periods.summary: The Qing leased the New Territories and islands for ninety-nine years in 1898. Villagers fought British troops during the April 1899 takeover. Meanwhile plague, coercive house searches and demolition, sanitation works and a permanent bacteriological laboratory transformed public health and state power.

periods.title: A global port under unequal colonial rule
periods.summary: After the Qing fell, refugees and commerce tied Hong Kong ever more closely to events in China and overseas. Schools, medicine, transport and business grew, while racial housing law, female bondservitude, low political representation and major worker strikes exposed the limits of the colony's prosperity.

periods.title: Atlas label changes; the colony continues
periods.summary: Nothing constitutional happened in 1938 to end Hong Kong. The atlas simply moves the same labelled shape from the hong-kong record to united-kingdom-1938, while British colonial administration continued until the Japanese invasion in December 1941.

periods.title: Japanese invasion and occupation
periods.summary: Japan attacked on 8 December 1941; the British governor surrendered on 25 December. During three years and eight months of military occupation, residents faced violence, hunger, rationing, coerced departure and forced exchange of Hong Kong dollars for military notes.

periods.title: Return, refugees, factories and public housing
periods.summary: British administration returned in 1945. Returnees and refugees drove extraordinary population growth; textile-led manufacturing replaced some lost China trade, while resettlement blocks, expanded schooling, hospitals, reservoirs and sanitation reshaped family life without erasing crowding or low-wage labour.

periods.title: Negotiated transition
periods.summary: The 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration set 30 June 1997 as the end of British administration and 1 July as China's resumption of sovereignty, with a Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and stated guarantees for its systems and way of life.

periods.title: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region
periods.summary: Hong Kong continues as an inalienable part and local administrative region of the People's Republic of China. The Basic Law provides a high degree of autonomy and separate executive, legislative and judicial powers within defined limits, while defence and foreign affairs belong to the central government.

sections.title: Read the atlas before the history

items.text: The indexed card says about 1650-1938, but all twelve hong-kong border files use nearly the same simplified present-day footprint. Point tests put Central, Kowloon, Sha Tin, Tai Po, Yuen Long, Sai Kung, Tai O and Lo Wu inside even in 1650, while the tested point on Cheung Chau falls outside. That is a display polygon, not evidence that one Hong Kong polity controlled this whole area for 288 years.

The record ends because of atlas bookkeeping. In 1938 the same shape becomes a Hong Kong-labelled feature of united-kingdom-1938; the atlas still assigns it there in 2000, after the real 1997 handover, and only assigns the labelled feature to china in 2010. The modern GeoJSON has no standalone hong-kong feature. Use the dates below for history, not these ownership labels.

Hong Kong Island entered the British Empire through war. Article III of the 1842 Treaty of Nanking says the Qing emperor ceded the island after Britain defeated China in the First Opium War, a conflict bound up with Britain's opium trade and demands for wider commerce. The treaty speaks for two empires; it records no vote by the island's villagers or boat families.

The colony grew in stages: Hong Kong Island was ceded in 1842, Kowloon south of Boundary Street in 1860, and the New Territories plus islands leased for ninety-nine years in 1898. These were different legal arrangements produced by imperial wars and pressure, so today's outline must not be projected backward as one timeless unit.

Local people did resist. When Britain imposed colonial rule in the New Territories, serious fighting between troops and inhabitants lasted from 14 to 19 April 1899. The surviving Old Tai Po Police Station also reveals the empire's layered workforce: its first staff included one European officer, seven Indian constables and one Chinese constable.

Colonial government was not representative democracy: a governor appointed from London worked with appointed councils, and the first Chinese Legislative Council member was not nominated until 1880. Seamen in 1922 and workers in the 1925-26 Canton-Hong Kong strike used collective action to challenge employers, colonial authority and an economy dependent on the port.

Racial hierarchy became literal housing law. The 1904 Peak District Reservation Ordinance prohibited owners and tenants, except by exemption, from letting residences in the defined hill district to Chinese people. The same Peak reached by a celebrated new tram was therefore also a landscape of wealth and legalized exclusion.

Some girls were transferred into wealthy households as mui tsai, female bondservants, and the practice provoked arguments among officials and Chinese elites over slavery, family custom and colonial power. The 1923 Female Domestic Service Ordinance declared that payment created no property right in a child and prohibited new mui tsai employment, though passing a law did not instantly erase exploitation.

The sheltered harbour powered an entrepot, a place where goods were imported, stored and re-exported. Before the colony, official estimates counted about 3,650 people across villages and hamlets and another 2,000 fishers living aboard boats. Port growth did not begin on empty land: British commerce overlaid an inhabited coast.

Population rose from 32,983 in 1851 to 878,947 in 1931, while recorded ocean-going shipping rose from 2,889 vessels in 1860 to 23,881 in 1939. Those figures show extraordinary port growth, but totals alone hide who loaded cargo, kept shops, raised children, endured low wages or accumulated the profits.

The built city mixed functions and styles. Completed about 1931, Lui Seng Chun placed a Chinese bone-setting medicine shop downstairs and the Lui family's rooms upstairs; its deep verandahs, reinforced concrete and neoclassical details suited both commerce and the subtropical climate. It is a useful household example, not a picture of every crowded tong lau.

A kid-sized engineering fact: the Peak Tram opened in 1888 with coal-powered steam machinery and cars for only thirty passengers. Its 1,278-metre route climbs grades as steep as 25.7 degrees, steep enough that the buildings outside can seem to lean, even though your seat is the thing tilting.

Qing and early colonial Hong Kong was never one village culture. Museum collections connect Punti and Hakka households especially with farming and ancestral halls, and Tanka, Hoklo and other boat-dwelling families especially with fishing, salted fish and junks. Clothing, work, belief and status varied within every label, and people moved between shore, harbour and wider Pearl River networks.

Wedding objects make family negotiation visible: a dowry register listed what a bride's family sent, food travelled in stacked gift boxes, and covered teacups served the groom's parents and relatives. These museum examples illuminate some Chinese customs without implying that every marriage, class or community followed the same script.

The colonial port drew communities from far beyond Britain and China. Muslim merchants and sailors from the Indian subcontinent arrived with maritime trade; Indian soldiers, police, prison guards and clerks also lived and worked in the colony. Jamia Mosque, rebuilt in 1915-16 with a Bombay merchant's donation, became a worship and gathering place rather than a decorative relic.

Urban geography reflected class and race. Late nineteenth-century Central held government, finance and many European-style buildings, while large numbers of Chinese residents crowded into tenements in West Point and Sheung Wan. This was a common pattern, not an airtight separation: Chinese merchants, Eurasian families, Portuguese, South Asian and other residents made the city more complicated than two camps.

Postwar resettlement could mean a family of five or more in about 120 square feet, with no private kitchen or bathroom. At Shek Kip Mei, neighbours cooked and washed clothes along shared corridors and used communal toilets and washing areas in the connecting block. The concrete buildings reduced fire danger, but privacy was definitely not included in the starter package.

Village education could be clan-based and selective. At Yi Tai Study Hall, young Tang clansmen studied the Thousand Character Classic, Three Character Classic, Four Books and Five Classics with locally hired or Guangdong teachers. Students were nicknamed the “Students of White Stone Lane”; the hall later became a small primary school and stopped teaching during the 1941 occupation.

Colonial schooling added other routes but remained unequal. Central School opened in 1862 for Chinese boys, combining Chinese classics with English and mathematics. Girls' formal schooling depended mainly on women missionaries and nuns until the government Central School for Girls opened in 1890, so sex, money, religion and family expectations shaped who could study.

Higher education also arrived gradually: the Hong Kong College of Medicine began in 1887; HKU was incorporated in 1911 and admitted its first Arts, Engineering and Medicine students in 1912. Women were first admitted in 1921. These milestones created opportunity, but a university seat still reached only a tiny share of young people.

A Qing inscription you can still see in the heritage record is 進士. In modern Cantonese Jyutping it is zeon3 si6; Mandarin pinyin is jìnshì. It means a successful candidate at the highest imperial examination level, rendered by the heritage booklet as “Graduate of the Palace Examination.” The plaque honoured Tang Man-wai, who passed in 1685, and advertised learning as family prestige.

A precisely dated modern document gives a longer language sample. Basic Law Article 1 (promulgated in 1990, effective in 1997) reads: 香港特別行政區是中華人民共和國不可分離的部分。 Jyutping: Hoeng1 Gong2 Dak6 Bit6 Hang4 Zing3 Keoi1 si6 Zung1 Waa4 Jan4 Man4 Gung6 Wo4 Gwok3 bat1 ho2 fan1 lei4 dik1 bou6 fan6. Official English: “The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region is an inalienable part of the People's Republic of China.” This is Traditional-character Modern Standard Written Chinese read here in Cantonese, not a transcript of casual speech.

Chinese residents built institutions of their own. Tung Wah Hospital was founded by ordinance in 1870 and opened in 1872, offering free Chinese medicine to sick and poor people; its leaders also organized relief, burial help, repatriation and later a free school. Community leadership mattered, though wealthy directors did not speak for every Chinese resident.

The 1894 bubonic plague killed at least 2,500 people that year. Army and police teams searched homes, removed patients and bodies, disinfected flats, and authorities later cleared nearly 400 apartment blocks around Tai Ping Shan. These measures helped build public-health capacity, but frightened families also experienced intrusion, flight, loss of housing and unequal blame.

The outbreak also became a global scientific turning point. Shibasaburo Kitasato and Alexandre Yersin arrived in June 1894 and independently identified a bacterium associated with plague. Historians still debate priority because Kitasato reported first but Yersin's description better matches the organism later called Yersinia pestis, so the honest discovery story has two laboratories, rivalry and uncertainty.

In 1906 the government opened a permanent Bacteriological Institute, Hong Kong's first purpose-built public-health laboratory. Its red-brick Edwardian shell, arcaded verandah and Chinese tiled roof show science and architecture adapting to a humid climate; the building later made vaccines and now houses the Hong Kong Museum of Medical Sciences.

sections.title: Water, toilets and the very practical city

items.text: Fresh water was a stubborn limit. Early residents drew from streams and wells; free public wells began in 1851, Pok Fu Lam became the first impounding reservoir in 1863, and the Tai Tam works added storage and filtration. Engineers kept enlarging the system because population and dry seasons repeatedly outran supply.

Toilet history is gloriously unglamorous. Many Chinese households used wooden waste buckets carried away by hand, while some privately run public toilets collected the contents to sell as farm fertilizer. Yes: somebody could literally own a poop business. European houses more often had early water closets, but scarce water, bad drains and disease made neither system automatically safe.

The Sanitary Board created after Chadwick's 1882 report supervised waste and toilet reform, while the city used combined drains in which stormwater carried sewage toward surrounding waters. This was infrastructure, but not modern treatment: dense construction, flooding and direct discharge kept creating health and pollution problems.

After plague, Pound Lane Public Bathhouse opened in 1904 as Hong Kong's first public bathhouse. A bathhouse was serious public-health technology for families whose homes had no bathroom: washing bodies and clothes outside crowded rooms could matter as much as a laboratory microscope.

Occupation reached kitchens and rooftops. Japanese authorities rationed rice, coerced people to leave, and forced exchange into military notes; archival records show residents queueing for food and growing vegetables on roofs. Experiences differed, civilians, internees, prisoners, collaborators and resistance members faced distinct dangers, but hunger touched much of the city.

After surrender, people returned at extraordinary speed and new refugees arrived from China's civil war: official estimates put the population near 600,000 in August 1945, 1.8 million by the end of 1947 and 2.2 million by mid-1950. Textile mills and then garments helped turn a trading port into a manufacturing city powered by migrant capital, skills and abundant low-paid labour.

The 1953 Shek Kip Mei fire left about 58,000 people homeless and pushed government into mass concrete resettlement. The programme reduced dangerous squatting and later added self-contained flats, but the first blocks offered only tiny rooms and shared sanitation. Achievement and limitation lived on the same corridor.

The 1984 Joint Declaration did not simply renew the New Territories lease. Britain agreed to restore all Hong Kong to China on 1 July 1997, and China set out an HKSAR with a high degree of autonomy, separate economic and legal arrangements, and policies stated to remain unchanged for fifty years. British colonial rule ended; Hong Kong's people and city did not.

Under the Basic Law, Hong Kong is part of China and directly under the Central People's Government, while exercising specified executive, legislative and independent judicial powers. The central government handles defence and foreign affairs; the HKSAR handles local public order. That nested constitutional status is why “independent country,” “ordinary Chinese city” and “British colony after 1997” are all misleading labels.

ending.text: The atlas's hong-kong record stops in 1938, but Hong Kong did not. British colonial administration continued, interrupted by Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945, until the 1997 handover. Hong Kong continues today as a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China under the Basic Law; the atlas's later United Kingdom and China labels are coarse display assignments, not substitute constitutional history.
